title: SVM II — Soft Margin & the C Parameter

blocks.t: From the notes
Soft margin, as written

Hard margin works only when the data is perfectly linearly
separable — which almost never happens.

Soft margin SVM allows some misclassification. We add a
slack $\xi_i$ for each point and pay a penalty $C\sum \xi_i$.
C is the penalty for misclassification:

items:
C large $\to$ less tolerance $\to$ narrow margin $\to$
overfitting.

C small $\to$ more tolerance $\to$ wide margin $\to$
underfitting.

blocks.t: Slack variables
Relax each hard constraint $y_i(w^Tx_i+b)\ge1$ by an amount $\xi_i\ge0$:

The slack $\xi_i$ measures how far past its own margin line point $i$
has intruded, in functional-margin units:
\xi_i = \max\big(0, 1-y_i(w^Tx_i+b)\big).

items: $\xi_i = 0$ — correctly classified, at or beyond the margin. Well behaved.

$0 < \xi_i \le 1$ — inside the margin but still on the correct side.
A margin violation, not an error.

blocks.t:
So $\sum_i \xi_i$ upper-bounds the number of training errors, and the objective
trades that bound against margin width.

blocks.cap:
Left: the three regimes of $\xi$. Middle: hinge loss compared with
log loss and 0–1 loss — note it is exactly zero once $z\ge1$, which is
what produces sparsity. Right: as $C$ grows both the margin and the number of
support vectors shrink.

blocks.t: Soft margin is hinge loss plus L2

At the optimum the constraints are tight, so $\xi_i = \max(0,1-y_i f(x_i))$
with $f(x)=w^Tx+b$. Substituting removes $\xi$ entirely:

\boxed{ \min_{w,b} \underbrace{\tfrac12\|w\|^2}_{\text{L2 regularisation}}
 + C\sum_{i=1}^{n}\underbrace{\max\big(0, 1-y_i f(x_i)\big)}_{\text{hinge loss}} }
Divide by $C$ and set $\lambda = \frac{1}{C}$ (up to a factor of $n$):
\min_{w,b} \sum_i \max(0,1-y_if(x_i)) + \frac{\lambda}{2}\|w\|^2 .
The single most useful sentence about $C$

A soft-margin SVM is regularised empirical risk minimisation with hinge
loss, and
C = \frac{1}{\lambda}.

So $C$ is the inverse of regularisation strength. Everything the notes
say follows immediately: large $C$ = weak regularisation = fits the training
data hard = overfits; small $C$ = strong regularisation = wide smooth margin =
underfits. If you already understand alpha in Ridge, you already
understand $C$ — it just runs the other way.

The comparison with logistic regression now becomes exact. Both minimise
"loss + L2". The only difference is the loss: log loss
$\log(1+e^{-z})$ is positive everywhere, so every point pulls on the
boundary; hinge loss $\max(0,1-z)$ is identically zero for $z\ge1$, so points
comfortably beyond the margin contribute nothing. That flat region is
the entire source of the SVM's sparsity.
The dual and the three kinds of support vector

Repeating the Lagrangian derivation of Topic 72 with the extra constraints
gives a dual that is identical except for one change — an upper bound
on each multiplier:

\max_{\alpha} \sum_i \alpha_i - \tfrac12\sum_i\sum_j \alpha_i\alpha_j y_iy_j
\langle x_i,x_j\rangle
\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad
\boxed{0 \le \alpha_i \le C},\quad \sum_i\alpha_iy_i=0 .

$C$ appears only as a ceiling on the $\alpha_i$ — the "box
constraint". That is why the soft-margin SVM costs nothing extra to solve, and
why the kernel trick of Topic 74 applies unchanged.
The KKT conditions then partition the training set into exactly three groups:

This partition is practically useful. $b$ must be computed from the
free support vectors only ($0<\alpha_i<C$), because they are the ones
that genuinely lie on the margin line. And the count of bounded support vectors
tells you how many points the model has decided to sacrifice — a direct read
of how noisy $C$ thinks your data is.

blocks.t:
$C$ must be tuned on a log scale — np.logspace(-3, 3, 13) —
never linearly. And it must be tuned after scaling, inside the same
pipeline: rescaling the features rescales $\|w\|$, which changes the effective
$C$ entirely. A $C$ tuned on unscaled data is meaningless on scaled data.

Large $C$ is also slow. Near the hard-margin regime the QP becomes
ill-conditioned and the SMO solver may hit max_iter without converging,
returning a silently poor model. If SVC appears to hang, your $C$ is
almost certainly too large — or your features are unscaled, which has the same
effect.
Class imbalance: per-class $C$
With class_weight, each class $k$ gets its own penalty $C_k = C\cdot w_k$:
\min \tfrac12\|w\|^2 + C\sum_{i: y_i=+1} w_{+}\xi_i + C\sum_{i: y_i=-1} w_{-}\xi_i .

class_weight="balanced" sets $w_k=\frac{n}{K\,n_k}$, so the rare class
gets a proportionally larger penalty and the boundary is pushed away from it.
The dual box constraint becomes $0\le\alpha_i\le C_{y_i}$ — again, just a
per-point ceiling.
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.svm import SVC, LinearSVC
from sklearn.linear_model import SGDClassifier
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, GridSearchCV, cross_val_score
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline, make_pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=1500, n_features=20, n_informative=8,
                           flip_y=0.12, class_sep=0.9, random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)

# ==================================================================
# 1. TUNING C -- on a LOG scale, with the scaler inside the pipeline
# ==================================================================
pipe = Pipeline([("sc", StandardScaler()),
                 ("svm", SVC(kernel="linear"))])

gs = GridSearchCV(pipe, {"svm__C": np.logspace(-3, 3, 13)},
                  cv=5, scoring="accuracy", n_jobs=4, return_train_score=True)
gs.fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("best C:", gs.best_params_["svm__C"], " CV:", round(gs.best_score_, 4))

# Read the bias-variance story straight off the grid:
for C, tr, te in zip(gs.cv_results_["param_svm__C"],
                     gs.cv_results_["mean_train_score"],
                     gs.cv_results_["mean_test_score"]):
    print(f"C={float(C):8.3f}  train {tr:.4f}  cv {te:.4f}  gap {tr-te:+.4f}")

# ==================================================================
# 2. INSPECTING THE THREE KINDS OF SUPPORT VECTOR
# ==================================================================
C = 1.0
m = SVC(kernel="linear", C=C).fit(StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xtr), ytr)

alpha = np.abs(m.dual_coef_).ravel()          # sklearn stores alpha_i * y_i
free    = (alpha > 1e-8) & (alpha < C - 1e-8) # ON the margin, xi = 0
bounded = alpha >= C - 1e-8                   # violators, xi > 0
print(f"total points      : {len(ytr)}")
print(f"support vectors   : {len(m.support_)}")
print(f"  free (on margin): {free.sum()}")
print(f"  bounded (xi > 0): {bounded.sum()}")
print(f"non-SVs           : {len(ytr) - len(m.support_)}")

# Slack for every training point, computed by hand
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xtr)
f  = m.decision_function(Xs)
y_pm = np.where(ytr == 1, 1.0, -1.0)
xi = np.maximum(0.0, 1.0 - y_pm * f)
print("sum of slack:", round(xi.sum(), 2),
      "| margin violations:", int((xi > 0).sum()),
      "| actual errors:",     int((xi > 1).sum()))
print("training errors agree:", (xi > 1).sum() == (m.predict(Xs) != ytr).sum())

# ==================================================================
# 3. SOFT MARGIN == HINGE LOSS + L2  -- verified three ways
# ==================================================================
# (a) the SVC objective, evaluated by hand
w = m.coef_[0]
obj = 0.5 * w @ w + C * xi.sum()
print("primal objective:", round(obj, 3))

# (b) LinearSVC minimises the same thing with a different solver (liblinear)
lin = LinearSVC(C=C, loss="hinge", max_iter=20000).fit(Xs, ytr)
print("LinearSVC agrees:", round(lin.score(Xs, ytr), 4), round(m.score(Xs, ytr), 4))

# (c) SGDClassifier with hinge loss and alpha = 1/(C*n) is the SAME MODEL,
#     fitted by stochastic gradient descent -- the scalable route for big data.
sgd = SGDClassifier(loss="hinge", alpha=1.0 / (C * len(ytr)),
                    max_iter=5000, tol=1e-4, random_state=0).fit(Xs, ytr)
print("SGD hinge  :", round(sgd.score(Xs, ytr), 4))

# ==================================================================
# 4. CLASS IMBALANCE -- per-class C
# ==================================================================
Xi, yi = make_classification(n_samples=3000, n_features=15, n_informative=7,
                             weights=[0.93, 0.07], flip_y=0.02, random_state=1)
Xa, Xb, ya, yb = train_test_split(Xi, yi, test_size=0.3, stratify=yi, random_state=0)

for cw in (None, "balanced", {0: 1, 1: 20}):
    mm = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                       SVC(kernel="linear", C=1.0, class_weight=cw)).fit(Xa, ya)
    p = mm.predict(Xb)
    print(f"class_weight={str(cw):12s}",
          classification_report(yb, p, output_dict=True, zero_division=0)["1"])

# ==================================================================
# 5. WHICH IMPLEMENTATION TO USE
# ==================================================================
# SVC          : kernel-capable, O(n^2)-O(n^3). Fine up to ~10-20k rows.
# LinearSVC    : linear only, liblinear, scales to ~1e5-1e6 rows. NOTE it
#                penalises the intercept and defaults to squared_hinge.
# SGDClassifier: loss="hinge", scales to millions / out-of-core via partial_fit.
#                alpha = 1/(C*n_samples) maps SGD's regularisation onto SVC's C.
#
# All three optimise the SAME objective; they differ only in solver and scale.

# ==================================================================
# 6. SOFT MARGIN FOR REGRESSION -- SVR and the epsilon-tube
# ==================================================================
from sklearn.svm import SVR
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
Xr, yr = make_regression(n_samples=800, n_features=10, noise=15, random_state=0)
# epsilon defines a tube: errors smaller than epsilon cost NOTHING (the
# regression analogue of hinge loss's flat region). C prices the rest.
svr = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                    SVR(kernel="linear", C=10.0, epsilon=1.0)).fit(Xr[:600], yr[:600])
print("SVR R2:", round(svr.score(Xr[600:], yr[600:]), 4))
Everything on one page
Summary

Problem: $\min \frac12\|w\|^2 + C\sum_i \xi_i$ subject to
$y_i(w^Tx_i+b)\ge 1-\xi_i$, $\xi_i\ge0$.

Slack: $\xi_i=\max(0,1-y_if(x_i))$. Zero = fine, in $(0,1]$ = inside
the margin but still correct, $>1$ = misclassified.

Equivalent form: hinge loss + L2, with $C=1/\lambda$. $C$ is
inverse regularisation strength.

Dual: identical to the hard-margin dual but with the box constraint
$0\le\alpha_i\le C$.

Three kinds of point: $\alpha_i=0$ (ignored), $0<\alpha_i<C$ (free SV,
sits on the margin, used to compute $b$), $\alpha_i=C$ (bounded SV, a
violator).

$C$ large $\to$ narrow margin, few SVs, low bias/high variance,
approaches the hard margin. $C$ small $\to$ wide margin, many SVs,
high bias/low variance.

Practice: scale first, tune $C$ on a log grid inside the pipeline, use
class_weight for imbalance, and switch to LinearSVC or
SGDClassifier(loss="hinge") beyond about 20k rows.
Interview corner
Q. What does $C$ control?

The price of margin violations. It is the inverse of regularisation strength:
the soft-margin objective is hinge loss $+\;\frac{1}{2C}\|w\|^2$ after
rescaling. Large $C$ = weak regularisation = narrow margin = overfit; small $C$
= strong regularisation = wide margin = underfit.
Q. What is a slack variable?

$\xi_i \ge 0$ measuring how far point $i$ intrudes past its own margin line, in
functional-margin units. $\xi_i \in (0,1]$ means it is inside the margin but
still correctly classified; $\xi_i > 1$ means it is on the wrong side.
Q. How does the dual change from hard to soft margin?

Only by the upper bound: $\alpha_i \le C$ instead of $\alpha_i$ unbounded. The
objective is unchanged, which is why kernels apply identically.
Q. What is the difference between a free and a bounded support vector?

Free ($0<\alpha_i<C$) lies exactly on the margin with $\xi_i=0$ — these are
used to recover $b$. Bounded ($\alpha_i=C$) has $\xi_i>0$ and lies inside the
margin or on the wrong side; the optimiser has capped its influence.
Q. How is an SVM related to logistic regression?

Both minimise a convex loss plus L2. Hinge loss is exactly zero beyond the
margin, so only nearby points matter and the solution is sparse in support
vectors; log loss is positive everywhere, so all points contribute and the
output is a calibrated probability. Hinge is not a proper scoring rule, which
is why SVC needs Platt scaling to produce probabilities.
Q. Why is probability=True discouraged in SVC?

It runs internal 5-fold cross-validation to fit a Platt sigmoid, making training
roughly five times slower, and the resulting probabilities can be inconsistent
with predict() (the argmax of the probabilities may disagree with the
sign of the decision function). Use decision_function for ranking, or
CalibratedClassifierCV if you genuinely need probabilities.
Q. Number of support vectors: what does it tell you?

It is a rough capacity measure — the leave-one-out error is bounded by
$\#\text{SV}/n$. Nearly all points being support vectors means $C$ is too small
or the kernel is too wide (heavy underfitting); very few means $C$ is large and
the model may be brittle.
Q. How do you scale SVMs to a million rows?

Not with SVC — its kernel solver is between $O(n^2)$ and $O(n^3)$. Use
LinearSVC for linear problems, SGDClassifier(loss="hinge") for
out-of-core, or approximate the kernel explicitly with Nystroem or
RBFSampler followed by a linear model.
Worked Examples
Soft margin: the $C$ trade-off in numbers
Soft-margin objective: $\tfrac12\|w\|^2 + C\sum_i \max(0,\;1-y_i f(x_i))$. The hinge term is $\max(0,1-m)$ where $m = y f(x)$ is the margin.
Step 1 – hinge losses. Four points with margins $m = [1.5,\;1.0,\;0.4,\;-0.5]$ have hinge losses $[0,\;0,\;0.6,\;1.5]$, total $2.1$.
Step 2 – two candidate hyperplanes.

blocks.t: At $C=0.1$ the wide-margin candidate W wins: the cost of misclassification is small, so the optimiser keeps the margin wide.
Step 3 – raise $C$ to 10. W costs $0.5 + 10\cdot 2.1 = 21.5$, N costs $4.0$. Now N wins: each violation is expensive, so the model bends the margin to fit every point.
Reading the table. Small $C$ $\Rightarrow$ wide margin, more tolerated errors (high bias). Large $C$ $\Rightarrow$ narrow margin, few errors on training data (high variance).
